assessments.title: Crafter Master Branch Safety Check
assessments.quote: In order to ensure that no malicious maintenance pull requests have been merged, the Crafter must check that the latest commit made to the "master" (or "main") branch of the Spell repository is the commit that merged the last Spell to master.
assessments.description: Requires the Crafter to confirm the latest master/main commit equals the commit that merged the last Spell before proceeding.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The check is a defined actor performing a verifiable comparison of commit identity on a named branch, so a third party could test compliance from the text. It lacks a stated cadence or failure response, and the master/main ambiguity is left unresolved.
metrics: Latest commit on the "master" (or "main") branch must equal the commit that merged the last Spell to master
assessments.enforcementReasoning: Emergency Spells can freeze or pause execution when security rules are violated or threatened, which would reach a malicious merge the check is meant to catch. Escalation depends on someone detecting that the check was skipped or failed, and the Crafter's own performance of the check is self-policed.

assessments.title: Tests Must Pass Before Crafter Provides Spell to Reviewers
assessments.quote: Before marking a Spell’s Pull Request as "ready for review", the Crafter must ensure that both continuous integration tests and locally run tests are all passing successfully. The only exception to this rule is when the continuous integration tests are broken at no fault of the Spell Team - due to a GitHub failure or otherwise - in which case the Spell can be marked as "ready for review" if locally run tests are passing. The Crafter must not remove or disable failing tests in order to bypass this rule.
assessments.description: Requires Spell Crafters to have all CI and local tests passing before marking a Spell pull request ready for review, with a CI-outage exception.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The core obligation is objectively checkable: all CI and local tests must pass before the ready-for-review flag is set, and tests may not be removed or disabled. The CI-outage exception is weaker, since 'at no fault of the Spell Team' and 'or otherwise' leave the trigger open to judgment, and no cadence or verification step is stated.
metrics: All continuous integration tests passing before marking PR 'ready for review'
All locally run tests passing before marking PR 'ready for review'
Exception only if CI is broken not at fault of the Spell Team, then local tests must pass
No removal or disabling of failing tests to bypass the rule
assessments.enforcementReasoning: Agent Artifact Review By Core GovOps (d4bf73e7) is a scheduled review with staged findings and penalty assessment that could catch a Spell marked ready with failing tests, with Core GovOps as an enforcer distinct from the Crafter. No quantified consequence is attached to this specific rule, and the review only fires if reviewers or GovOps surface the violation.

assessments.title: Process For Handling Technical Issues
assessments.quote: The Crafter plays a key role in the process for identifying, analyzing, and resolving technical issues like bugs, mistakes, and exploits when they arise during the Spell development process. Other stakeholders, including the Spell Reviewer and Core Facilitator, also play an important role. This process is set out in the subdocuments herein.
assessments.description: Assigns the Spell Crafter a role in identifying, analyzing, and resolving technical issues during spell development, with other stakeholders involved, detailed elsewhere.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The paragraph names actors (Crafter, Spell Reviewer, Core Facilitator) but gives no thresholds, steps, deadlines, or criteria; it merely defers to subdocuments. It is a posture statement with no verifiable obligation in its own text.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. The paragraph states no consequence; only the generic misalignment and adjudication backstops could reach a failure to follow the process, and those are catch-all mechanisms that are weak alone.

assessments.title: Issue Detection and Classification
assessments.quote: When a technical issue is encountered, the party discovering the issue (whether the Crafter, a Reviewer, or another party) must determine whether the issue is either a mistake, a bug, or an exploit. The issue should also be classified as either a result of collusion or a genuine accident. The Spell Team must notify the Core Facilitator of technical issues that require input or adjustments from outside the Spell Team. Note that if a Crafter makes an error in their original development of the Spell, but discovers their own mistake and corrects it before the Reviewers commence the review process, this should not be treated as a technical issue per this handling process.
assessments.description: Requires discovering parties to classify technical issues as mistake, bug, or exploit, and Spell Teams to notify the Core Facilitator of issues needing outside input.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The obligations to classify the issue and notify the Core Facilitator are clear, but the classification has no criteria for distinguishing mistake, bug, exploit, collusion, or accident. The notification trigger ('requires input or adjustments from outside the Spell Team') and its timing are unquantified, so compliance is arguable on the same facts.
metrics: Carve-out applies only if the Crafter corrects their own error before the Reviewers commence the review process
assessments.enforcementReasoning: Agent Artifact Review by Core GovOps can examine Spell Team outputs and assess penalties, so a misclassified or unreported issue could surface there. The Emergency Response System provides an escalation path for security issues, but the consequence for this specific rule is not quantified and firing depends on someone raising the escalation.

assessments.title: Issue Analysis and Evidence Capture
assessments.quote: Once a technical issue has been categorized as an instance of a mistake, bug or exploit, the party discovering the issue must prepare documentation of the issue. This generally involves investigating the impacts of the issue, determining how the issue arose, and documenting how the issue manifests. In cases where the issue may be non-technical in nature - such as possible instances of collusion - supporting evidence should be captured, which supports the argument that a non-technical issue may be present. This evidence should be captured in a manner that does not permit bad actors to manipulate or erase the evidence through methods such as editing or deleting messages.
assessments.description: Requires the discovering party to document categorized technical issues and capture tamper-resistant evidence of suspected non-technical issues like collusion.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: A real documentation obligation exists ("must prepare documentation"), but its scope is hedged ("generally involves"), evidence capture is only "should", and the tamper-resistance requirement names no method, deadline, or verifiable standard. Compliance is arguable on the same facts.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No catalog mechanism watches whether issue documentation is prepared or evidence is preserved; the only reachable paths are the catch-all Reports of Misalignment and Adjudication Process, which alone are weak.

assessments.title: Determining the Handling Party
assessments.quote: Once a technical issue has been classified and evidence supporting its existence is collected, an entity needs to be designated as the handling party for resolving the issue. This party will typically be the Core Facilitator. However, if there is a non-trivial chance that the Core Facilitator will ignore or downplay the issue, another entity should serve as the handling party.
assessments.description: Assigns a handling party for classified technical issues, usually the Core Facilitator, unless it may downplay them.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The obligation to designate a handling party is real, but the switch-over trigger is judgment language ("non-trivial chance") with no probability or evidence threshold. The substitute entity is never identified, so compliance is arguable on the same facts.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No penalty, conservatorship, or emergency mechanism is triggered by a failure to designate a proper handling party; only the generic misalignment and adjudication backstops apply.

assessments.title: Publicly Reporting the Issue
assessments.quote: Discovered issues must be reported publicly unless doing so poses a threat to the security of the Sky Protocol. Technical issues that are currently or likely to become, actively exploitable must not be discussed in a public manner, as this poses a threat to the security of the Sky Protocol.
assessments.description: Requires public reporting of discovered issues unless disclosure threatens protocol security, and bars public discussion of exploitable technical issues.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The obligation is real, but it turns on undefined judgment terms: 'threat to the security', 'currently or likely to become actively exploitable', and 'publicly'. No deadline, cadence, severity threshold, or responsible party is stated, so compliance is arguable on the same facts.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No penalty, emergency, or review mechanism is tied to disclosure decisions. Emergency Spells and Emergency Response System could respond to exploitable issues, but nothing in the text links them to this reporting rule, so only the generic misalignment and adjudication backstops apply.

assessments.title: Resolving the Issue and Following Up
assessments.quote: The Crafter or Reviewer, if they discovered the technical issue, should address or remedy the issue as necessary to resolve it. The handling party (typically the Core Facilitator) must follow up to ensure that the technical issue has been resolved. If the issue poses a threat to the Sky Protocol - such as an exploit or instance of collusion - it should be followed up on as a matter of urgency by the handling party.
assessments.description: Requires the crafter or reviewer to remedy technical issues and the handling party to follow up, with urgency for threats.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: A real obligation exists for the handling party to follow up on resolution, but it uses judgment language ("should address or remedy as necessary", "as a matter of urgency") with no deadline, cadence, or threshold defining what counts as a threat or as resolved.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: The Emergency Response System and Emergency Spells plausibly reach the urgent case where the issue is an exploit or collusion threat, but no consequence is quantified for failing to remedy or follow up on routine technical issues, and escalation depends on the handling party raising it.

assessments.title: Issue Retrospective
assessments.quote: Following the resolution of a technical issue, the parties involved in the development process, or other relevant processes leading to the issue arising, must document how the issue arose. These parties (often the Crafter or Reviewer) should also detail any measures that were previously in place to prevent this type of issue occurring, and any measures that can be implemented going forward in order to prevent the same issue from occurring again in the future.
assessments.description: Requires parties to a technical issue to document its cause, prior preventive measures, and future prevention steps.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The obligation to document is clear and the required content is enumerated, but there is no deadline for 'following the resolution', no format or depth standard, and the responsible parties are hedged ('often the Crafter or Reviewer'). Compliance could be argued either way on the same facts.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No penalty, escalation, or review mechanism is tied to retrospective documentation. Only the generic misalignment-reporting and adjudication backstops could reach a missing retrospective, and those alone are weak. Agent Artifact Review (d4bf73e7) could arguably cover Crafter artifacts, but the paragraph does not place retrospectives within that review scope.

assessments.title: Spell Team Operational Principles
assessments.quote: As a core member of the Spell Team, the Crafter must comply with the Spell Team Operational Principles throughout their involvement in the Spell development process. These principles apply to both Spell crafting and Spell reviewing processes, and have been included in the documentation of both. These principles are set out in the subdocuments herein.
assessments.description: Requires the Spell Crafter, as a core Spell Team member, to comply with Spell Team Operational Principles defined in subdocuments.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The paragraph is a pure pointer: the operative principles are deferred to unnamed subdocuments with no metrics, thresholds, or criteria in this text. Nothing here can be checked against directly.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: none found. The paragraph itself names no consequence, and the principles it points to are not operative here; only the generic misalignment and adjudication backstops would apply.

assessments.title: Security First
assessments.quote: Any choice between efficiency and security must always be made to maximize security, even at the cost of time, process inefficiency, or gas cost. Smart contract system designs as well as individual smart contracts, their code, and their interactions must always prioritize increased security over increased efficiency, reduced gas cost, or any other benefits. Rules and processes must always maximize security and safety, even at the cost of inefficiency, repetitiveness, longer review or audit timelines, or other drawbacks.
assessments.description: States a general principle that security must take precedence over efficiency, gas cost, and timelines in design and rules.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The paragraph is a posture statement with no thresholds, metrics, formulas, or verifiable conditions. 'Maximize security' and 'prioritize security' cannot be checked against any defined standard, so there is nothing concrete to comply with.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No mechanism is triggered by a defined violation of this principle. Emergency Spells and Artifact Review could in principle reach specific security failures, but the paragraph gives no criteria for what counts as a breach, so no escalation path is identifiable.

assessments.title: Attention to Detail
assessments.quote: Developing, modifying or reviewing code should be done line by line. No change, issue or fix is too minor or unimportant to be commented on or addressed. Sky Core Contracts are immutable, and disabling them often requires waiting for a long period. As such, bugs and exploits should never be present in production code, as they are typically difficult to fix and their presence harms the reputation of the Sky Protocol. Any deployed contract that contains a bug indicates that the existing quality control, auditing, and review processes are not adequately preventing bugs.
assessments.description: Requires developers to review code line by line and states that bugs should never reach production code.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The paragraph imposes a real review-process obligation but uses judgment language ('should be done line by line', 'should never be present') with no thresholds, cadence, or measurable criteria. A defender could argue it is mostly posture rather than a binding rule.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No mechanism is tied to line-by-line review or to bugs in deployed code. Emergency Spells and Agent Artifact Review could reach exploited bugs generally, but the paragraph states no consequence, so only the catch-all applies.

assessments.title: Minimizing Complexity
assessments.quote: Smart contract system designs, as well as individual smart contracts, their code, and their interactions must always use a simpler design over a more complex design, unless the more complex design provides a significant net increase to the safety and security of the Sky Protocol.
assessments.description: Requires smart contract designs and code to prefer simpler designs unless complexity yields a significant net security gain.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule names a clear obligation (prefer simpler designs) with an exception, but 'significant net increase to safety and security' has no metric, threshold, or assessment method, and no actor is assigned to judge it. Compliance on the same facts is arguable either way.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: No enforcement mechanism in the paragraph or catalog specifically reaches a design-simplicity violation; only the generic misalignment and adjudication backstops apply, so the rating is weak. Emergency Spells or Agent Artifact Review could plausibly catch egregious complexity, but nothing ties them to this rule.

assessments.title: Lindy-Based Risk Aversion
assessments.quote: The "Lindy Effect" states that the longer something has been in existence in its current state, the longer its remaining life expectancy. The "Lindy" of a system or smart contract refers to the duration it has been operating in its current state and therefore implies its future stability. Specifically, the "Lindy" of immutable systems uses their history of safe and secure operation as a predictor of future safety and security. It is considered best practice to consider the "Lindy" of systems, elements,and smart contracts when evaluating their use or inclusion in the wider system of the Sky Protocol.
assessments.description: States the Lindy Effect as a best-practice consideration when evaluating smart contracts and systems for Sky Protocol inclusion.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The paragraph is a posture statement that defines the Lindy concept and recommends it as best practice. It sets no threshold, metric, duration, or evaluation criteria, and 'consider' is non-binding judgment language.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No penalty, liquidation, emergency, or review mechanism attaches to a failure to consider Lindy; only the generic misalignment and adjudication backstops could apply.

assessments.title: Chesterton’s Fence
assessments.quote: Chesterton’s Fence is a principle that states that changes must not be made to the current state of affairs unless the reasoning behind the current state of affairs is understood and can be explained. Changes to the Sky Protocol must only be proposed after the context - such as the reasoning, actions, and history - leading to the thing’s current state are known and can be explained by the party proposing the change. Changes must not be approved by team members or otherwise accepted until all parties responsible for overseeing, checking, or reviewing the change are aware of the context behind the current state of affairs as it exists before the change is enacted.
assessments.description: Requires that changes to the Sky Protocol be proposed and approved only after their existing context is known, explained, and shared with reviewers.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The paragraph states a real sequencing obligation (context must be known before proposal, and reviewers must be aware before approval), but it relies on judgment terms like "understood," "can be explained," and "aware" with no defined standard, documentation requirement, or verification method. A defender could reasonably argue compliance on the same facts either way.
metrics: Changes must only be proposed after the context (reasoning, actions, and history) behind the current state is known and can be explained by the proposer
Changes must not be approved or accepted until all parties overseeing, checking, or reviewing the change are aware of the pre-change context
Awareness of context must occur before the change is enacted
assessments.enforcementReasoning: Agent Artifact Review by Core GovOps (A.1.14.2.10) is a scheduled review with staged findings and penalty assessment, and it could plausibly catch a change proposed or approved without the required context. The rule does not quantify any consequence specific to it, and firing depends on reviewers escalating the omission.

assessments.title: Existing Process Adherence
assessments.quote: All existing Sky processes and patterns, whether pertaining to rules, processes, systems, smart contracts, or code, must be complied with. If regular operation is impossible due to a technical limitation or otherwise, it is permitted so long as it does not compromise the safety or security of the Sky Protocol in any way. New patterns developed in this way must prioritize the safety and security of the Sky Protocol over all other considerations and should be as similar to old patterns as possible. However, deviation from industry norms and best practices is encouraged so long as they are made in the interest of maximizing security. Any deviations by the Crafter or Reviewers must be communicated to the Core Facilitator.
assessments.description: Requires existing Sky processes to be followed, permits safety-preserving deviations for new patterns, and requires deviations to be reported to the Core Facilitator.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: Named actors (Crafter, Reviewers, Core Facilitator) and a reporting duty exist, but the core standards are judgment language: 'should be as similar as possible', 'prioritize safety', and 'in any way'. No threshold, cadence, or deadline for communicating deviations is stated, so compliance is arguable.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: Emergency Spells (A.1.10.5) can pre-authorize intervention when a deviation threatens security, and Agent Artifact Review by Core GovOps could reach an unreported or unsafe spell-crafting deviation with penalty assessment. Neither is tied to this paragraph's terms, and escalation depends on someone raising the deviation.

assessments.title: Tenth Man Mandate
assessments.quote: If a group of people making a decision unanimously holds a certain opinion, all make the same assumption or all come to the same conclusion, it is the responsibility of one member of the group to assume that the rest of the group is incorrect. The member of the group assigned to hold this contrarian viewpoint is referred to as the ‘tenth man’ and must attempt to disprove the group’s decision. Where the ‘tenth man’ is able to provide compelling arguments against the group’s conclusion, the decision must be reassessed.
assessments.description: Requires a designated 'tenth man' to argue against unanimous group decisions, forcing reassessment if the counterargument is compelling.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The trigger (unanimity) and the actor (one designated member) are defined, but 'compelling arguments' has no criteria, and the rule sets no cadence, assignment procedure, or standard for when reassessment is complete. Compliance could be argued either way on the same facts.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. The paragraph sets no penalty or escalation for skipping the tenth man, and no catalog mechanism (penalties, artifact review, emergency spells) is tied to this process step. Enforcement depends on the group policing itself, which is self-enforcement and rates weak.

assessments.title: Providing Voters With Sufficient Information
assessments.quote:
The Core Facilitator must ensure that voters have access to sufficient information to make informed decisions. This might include:

- Links to documentation or discussions related to the actions included in the Executive Document.
- Summaries of the actions included in the Executive Document, created by unbiased and knowledgeable third parties.
- Links to any analysis published by DAO-funded entities regarding the actions in the Executive Document.
- Links to well-maintained resources describing the nature of any parameters that may be changed if the Executive Proposal passes.

Providing accessible and complete information is essential to maintaining the legitimacy of the process. Voters should not later regret their vote due to a lack of understanding of the actions they voted on.
assessments.description: Requires the Core Facilitator to ensure voters have sufficient information on Executive Document actions, with non-exhaustive examples.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The obligation is real (the Core Facilitator must ensure voter access), but 'sufficient' and 'complete' are undefined, and the listed resources are introduced with 'might include' and have no thresholds, deadlines, or verifiable criteria. Compliance is arguable either way on the same facts.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No penalty, conservatorship, or on-chain mechanism reaches a failure to inform voters, and Agent Artifact Review (d4bf73e7) and the Reports Of Misalignment catch-all do not specifically target this duty.

assessments.title: Ensuring Transparency And Clarity
assessments.quote:
The Core Facilitator must ensure that the Executive Document is clear, transparent, and accessible to all voters. This involves eliminating ambiguity and confusion to the greatest extent possible while balancing technical detail with readability. Voters should clearly understand:

- The effects and impacts of the Executive Vote if passed.
- The processes that led to each item being included in the Executive Document.
- The identities (pseudonymous or entity-level) of those responsible for publishing, writing, and reviewing the Executive Vote.

The goal is to ensure that voters are always provided with information on why an item is included, what will happen if the Executive Vote passes, or who is responsible for its contents.

Clarity reduces the risk of disruption, confusion, or a breakdown of legitimacy in the governance process.
assessments.description: Requires the Core Facilitator to make the Executive Document clear and transparent, covering vote effects, inclusion processes, and responsible parties.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The obligation is real and lists three content categories voters must understand, but it relies on judgment language such as "to the greatest extent possible" and "clearly understand" with no measurable clarity standard. Compliance could be argued either way on the same facts.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: Agent Artifact Review by Core GovOps can plausibly reach a Facilitator-produced Executive Document and assess penalties, with enforcer distinct from actor. The consequence is not quantified for clarity failures, and no mechanism specifically targets this duty.

assessments.title: Balancing Technical Detail And Accessibility
assessments.quote:
The Core Facilitator must ensure that the Executive Document balances technical detail with readability. Voters should not require in-depth technical knowledge of the Sky Protocol to understand the Executive Document.
Guidelines for Technical Detail:

- Avoid including excessive technical details that obscure clarity or clutter the Executive Document.
- Include technical details only when they are strictly necessary, such as:
    - In emergency or urgent responses when technical details are the primary focus of the proposal.
    - For non-urgent technical fixes or housekeeping when technical details are relevant, but should be given lower priority compared to other actions in the Executive Vote.

In cases where technical details are included, the Governance Point must ensure they fully understand the technical aspects themselves to present them accurately and clearly.

Excessive technical detail can overwhelm voters and obscure the document's primary purpose. By carefully managing technical content, the Core Facilitator ensures that the document remains accessible and focused.
assessments.description: Requires the Core Facilitator to balance technical detail with readability in Executive Documents, limiting technical content to necessary cases.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule relies on judgment language such as 'balances', 'excessive', and 'fully understand' with no numeric thresholds, length limits, or verifiable test. It does name two categories where technical detail is permitted (emergency/urgent responses and non-urgent housekeeping), but compliance on the same document could be argued either way.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No penalty, conservatorship, or on-chain mechanism reaches the readability of an Executive Document. Artifact Review (d4bf73e7) covers agent artifacts rather than this facilitator duty, so only the catch-all backstops remain.

assessments.title: Executive Summary
assessments.quote:
The Executive Summary outlines the key actions that will occur if the proposal passes. It includes:

- The GSM Pause Delay, which specifies the minimum time before the Spell can be executed and is enforced by ds-pause.
- The Office-Hours Modifier, if applicable, which restricts execution to specific times.
- The Expiration Date of the Spell.
    - The Spell must always have an expiration date; it can’t be more than 90 days in the future, and the typical expiration window is 30 days.
- A high-level explanation of the actions being performed in the Spell, presented in bullet-point form.

The summary should provide a high-level overview of the Executive Vote and ensure that SKY holders can quickly understand the scope and purpose of the proposal. This section also explains that voting for the proposal with SKY places support for these actions.
assessments.description: Specifies required contents of the Executive Summary, including GSM pause delay, office-hours modifier, and a spell expiration of at most 90 days.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The 90-day maximum expiration is a hard numeric bound, but the 30-day expiration is only a 'typical' window, the GSM Pause Delay has no stated value, and the office-hours modifier applies 'if applicable'. The 'high-level' explanation has no criteria.
metrics: Spell expiration date must always be set
Spell expiration no more than 90 days in the future
Typical expiration window of 30 days
GSM Pause Delay specifies minimum time before execution (value not stated)
assessments.enforcementReasoning: The paragraph governs the content of a disclosure summary, and no mechanism reaches the accuracy or completeness of that summary. The underlying GSM delay and spell expiry are on-chain, but they enforce the spell's execution, not the summary's contents. Only the catch-all misalignment reporting applies.

assessments.title: Core Facilitator Creates Executive Document
assessments.quote: The Core Facilitator must create the Executive Document. The subdocuments herein provide a step-by-step guide to the document’s creation.
assessments.description: Requires the Core Facilitator to create the Executive Document, following the referenced step-by-step subdocuments.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The paragraph names a defined actor and a concrete obligation, but gives no metric, deadline, or verifiable criteria for a complete document. The 'Week 2 Tuesday' timing appears only in the context heading, and the procedure is delegated to subdocuments.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No penalty, emergency, or artifact-review mechanism is tied to failing to create the Executive Document, so only the generic misalignment backstop reaches it.

assessments.title: Core Facilitator Reviews The Executive Sheet
assessments.quote: The Core Facilitator must thoroughly review the Executive Sheet. The technical information in the Executive Sheet must be identical to the Executive Document.
assessments.description: Requires the Core Facilitator to review the Executive Sheet and ensure its technical content matches the Executive Document.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The identity requirement between the Executive Sheet's technical information and the Executive Document is objectively checkable, but 'thoroughly review' is qualitative and 'technical information' is undefined. The Week 2 Tuesday deadline appears only in the context line, not the rule text.
metrics: Technical information in the Executive Sheet must be identical to the Executive Document
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No catalog mechanism targets Core Facilitator executive-document accuracy; Agent Artifact Review covers Agents, not the Facilitator, and the only generic backstops (Reports Of Misalignment, Adjudication) are catch-alls.

assessments.title: Core Facilitator Updates Metadata
assessments.quote:
The Core Facilitator must update the metadata of the template. This includes updating the filename and dates to reflect the current values of the Executive Vote.

- Rename the file to "Executive vote - YYYY, MONTH, DD". The filename must end with .md and must not contain any banned characters (e.g., "<>:"/?*|"). The date in the filename should correspond to the day the Executive Vote will go live on the voting platform.
- Replace the placeholder dates in the template with the correct dates for the Executive Vote. The exact time is not required for the Executive Vote and should therefore be left at midnight.
assessments.description: Requires the Core Facilitator to rename the executive vote file and set its dates to the vote's go-live date, using a defined naming format.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The filename pattern, .md extension, banned-character restriction, go-live date basis, and midnight time are all stated concretely and can be checked from the text. Gaps remain: the banned-character list is illustrative ("e.g."), the MONTH format and timezone are unspecified, and "current values" and "placeholder dates" are not defined.
metrics: Filename follows "Executive vote - YYYY, MONTH, DD"
Filename ends with .md
Filename contains no banned characters (e.g., <>:"/?*|)
Filename date equals the day the Executive Vote goes live on the voting platform
Placeholder dates in the template are replaced with the Executive Vote dates
Time is left at midnight
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No catalog mechanism reaches a filename or metadata error: the penalty, conservatorship, incident response, and artifact review mechanisms target Primes and agents rather than this procedural step, and emergency spells address security violations. Only the generic misalignment and adjudication backstops apply.

assessments.title: Core Facilitator Creates Title
assessments.quote: The Core Facilitator must create a title for the Executive Document that clearly highlights the most impactful/important actions included in the proposal. This ensures that SKY holders can easily understand the purpose of the vote.
assessments.description: Requires the Core Facilitator to title each Executive Document so it highlights the most important actions in the proposal.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: A real obligation with a named actor, but the standard is judgment-based: 'clearly highlights' and 'most impactful/important' have no measurable criteria, and no deadline or verification method is given. Compliance is arguable either way on the same title.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No penalty, artifact review, or on-chain mechanism targets title quality; the only reachable path is the generic misalignment backstop (c6c6f595), which is catch-all and does not make this rule enforceable.

assessments.title: Core Facilitator Creates Summary
assessments.quote:
The Core Facilitator must create a summary that refers to every action included in the proposal. Under the Executive summary, the Core Facilitator must include the following details:

1. Office-Hours Modifier:
    - If the office-hours parameter has the value "Yes" and will be present in the Spell code, this must be explicitly mentioned:
        - "This Executive Proposal includes an office-hours modifier that means that it **can only be executed between 14:00 and 21:00 UTC, Monday - Friday**."
2. GSM Pause Delay:
    - The GSM Pause Delay period and affected items must be clearly communicated.
    - The term "GSM Pause Delay" must include a link to the Atlas document specifying its definition [A.1.10.3.1 - Pause Delay](3c9545d9-775f-4149-88bf-7d297b5302c6).
    - The current value of the GSM Pause Delay must include a link to the Atlas document specifying its value [A.1.10.3.1.2 - Pause Delay Current Value](db442d8a-8d98-47a2-b162-01c2adc22b67).
3. Proposal Expiry:
    - The expiry of the proposal must be explicitly noted, including the length of time for which the proposal is valid:
        - "If this Executive Proposal does not pass within 30 days, then it will expire and can no longer have any effect on the Sky Protocol."

assessments.title: Core Facilitator Includes Every Item From Executive Sheet
assessments.quote:
The Core Facilitator must ensure that every item from the Executive Sheet is included in the details section of the Executive Document. These items should be presented in order of judged impact/importance. If the order of items in the Executive Document differs from the Executive Sheet, the Executive Sheet must be updated to match, maintaining consistency between the two documents.

The Core Facilitator must make sure that each item:

- Includes links to the reasoning and authorization for its inclusion.
- Provides additional links required for voters to understand the context surrounding the item’s inclusion.
- Uses future-conditional language and clearly outlines the actions that will take place if the Executive Proposal passes. For example, phrasing such as "If this Executive Proposal passes, then this action will take place" ensures clarity and avoids ambiguity.
- Has hyperlinked key parameters, terms, and contracts where appropriate, making it easier for voters to access relevant information. Ethereum and IPFS addresses should also be linked to provide direct access to technical details.

The Core Facilitator must also make sure that the parties implicated in the proposal outcome are aware of the wording used for each item in the Executive Document.

assessments.precisenessReasoning: The obligations are concrete: every Executive Sheet item must appear, the sheet must be updated on order mismatch, and each item needs links and future-conditional phrasing. assessments.title: Ecosystem Spell Validation Window
assessments.quote:
The Ecosystem Spell Validation Window is the period of time during which a Spell can be validated. Validation must occur:

1. After the Spell becomes visible and is available for voting on the Voting Portal (start of the validation window).
2. Before the Spell’s actions become executable, which occurs when the `GSM Pause Delay` elapses (end of the validation window).

Validation outside this window is ineffective because:

- The Spell may still be subject to changes before the start of the validation window.
- The Spell may already be executable after the end of the validation window.

The duration of the validation window is determined by the value of the GSM Pause Delay.
assessments.description: Defines when Ecosystem validators may validate a Spell: from its appearance on the Voting Portal until the GSM Pause Delay elapses.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The window start (Spell visible and available for voting on the Voting Portal) and end (GSM Pause Delay elapses) are defined events. The duration equals the GSM Pause Delay, a parameter defined elsewhere, but this paragraph gives no value or measurement cadence.

Window duration equals the value of the GSM Pause Delay
assessments.enforcementReasoning: Emergency Spells (A.1.10.5) provide pre-authorized executive intervention if a Spell threatens security during the window, which can reach a validation failure. The on-chain GSM delay only delays execution and does not enforce that validation occurs, and the paragraph states out-of-window validation is merely ineffective with no penalty.

assessments.title: Ecosystem Spell Verification Scope
assessments.quote:
The scope of Spell validation includes any code in the Sky Protocol that:

1. Must adhere to the `GSM Pause Delay` enforced by the Sky Protocol’s `ds-pause` contract, and
2. Is directly executed by the Sky Protocol’s `Pause Proxy` contract.

Actions that do not meet these criteria—such as `instant actions`, `MOM` and `IAM` contract calls—are excluded from Spell validation.

This exclusion is due to the absence of a pause delay for such actions, which prevents ecosystem actors from having sufficient time to perform their reviews.

Validators should also consider validating the source code or associated audits for contracts added to the Chainlog as part of a Spell, even if these contracts are not immediately executed or fall outside the standard validation scope. This includes pre-deployed emergency Spell contracts, ensuring that their integrity and security are assessed at the time of addition to the Chainlog for potential future use.

assessments.precisenessReasoning: The inclusion test is binary and checkable: code must follow the GSM Pause Delay and be directly executed by Pause Proxy. However, the GSM Pause Delay value is not stated, the exclusion list is open-ended ('such as'), and the Chainlog clause is hedged ('should also consider').

assessments.title: Spell Validators Must Ensure Tests Pass
assessments.quote:
Ecosystem Spell validators must execute the predefined tests associated with a Spell. These tests are provided as scripts in the Spell repository on GitHub. Validators must run these scripts to verify the correctness, security, and compatibility of the Spell. All tests must pass successfully—without errors or failures—for the Spell to pass validation.

The best practice for running the tests are specified herein:

1. If you haven’t cloned the repository before, run: `git clone <https://github.com/sky-ecosystem/Spells-mainnet`>.
2. Navigate to the Spell repository directory by running: `cd Spells-mainnet`.
3. Update the repository for the latest changes by running: `git pull`.
4. Switch to the correct branch by finding the name from the Spell’s pull request on GitHub, run the command: `git checkout NAME`.
5. Verify your setup and check that you’re on the correct branch by running: `git status`.
6. Clean up old Spell library dependencies by running the command: `rm -r lib` or deleting the `lib` folder and its contents.
7. Install libraries required for the current Spell by running `git submodule update --init --recursive`.
8. Configure the local or remote node being used by running `export ETH_RPC_URL=URL` with the URL of your local or remote node. If using a remote node, do not share the URL as it can be used maliciously.
9. Run the Spell tests by running `make test`. If there are concerns about potential modifications to the function, validators can bypass the `make` command and directly execute the test script using `./scripts/test-dssSpell-forge.sh`.
10. Wait for completion. Allow 20 to 60 minutes for the tests to complete.
11. Review and Save Results: Save the test results (pass or fail) for logging purposes.
assessments.description: Requires ecosystem Spell validators to run the repository's test scripts, ensure all tests pass, and save results.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The core obligation is objective: all tests must pass with no errors or failures, and a 20–60 minute runtime window and specific commands are given. Gaps remain: "correctness, security, and compatibility" are not defined, the bypass to ./scripts/test-dssSpell-forge.sh is conditional on unspecified "concerns", and the result-saving step has no format or retention period.

assessments.title: Spell Validators Must Check Deployed Spell Code
assessments.quote:
The Spell validator must ensure that the deployed Spell code matches the Spell code present in the GitHub Repository.

In order to pass validation, the deployed Spell must not contain any potentially malicious code or any notable functional changes within the `DssSpellAction`.

The validation for the Spell code can be done by using the `diff-deployed-Spell` script present in the Spell repository on GitHub to ensure that the deployed Spell’s code matches locally compiled code. Alternatively, an online tool like diff checker ([https://www.diffchecker.com/](https://www.diffchecker.com/)) can be used. The Spell code on Etherscan should be compared with the `DssSpell.sol` in the GitHub repository for the relevant Spell. If the Spell goes live before the code is merged to the main branch, it’s possible to find the branch by the Target Date name of the Spell (e.g., YYYY-MM-DD).

When comparing, note that the following differences are acceptable and should not be flagged (based on validation guides):

- Comments: Lines starting with `//` or inside `/* */`.
- Imports and Solidity versions: Multiple declarations in the GitHub code.
- Interfaces: Numerical suffixes like `_1` or `_2` added to interface names in the contract.
- DssExecLib Interface: Extra code or warnings within the `DssExecLib` library.
assessments.description: Requires Spell validators to confirm deployed Spell code matches the GitHub repository and contains no malicious or notable functional changes.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The obligation to diff deployed code against the GitHub source is concrete and checkable with named tools and a defined list of acceptable differences. The pass criteria, however, rely on judgment terms such as "potentially malicious" and "notable functional changes" with no defined standard.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. Penalty Mechanisms and Risk-Based Insurance Pricing target Primes and Operational Agents, not ecosystem validators. Emergency Spells (b8266c11) could halt a malicious Spell, but they do not reach a validator who fails to perform this check, so the rule rests on self-policing and the generic misalignment backstop.

assessments.title: Spell Validators Must Check Deployed Spell Is Not A DarkSpell
assessments.quote:
Validators must confirm that the deployed Spell does not execute an external `DssAction` contract. This validation ensures that the Spell is self-contained, does not rely on external contracts or pre-defined Ethereum addresses, and that the `DssExec` and `DssSpellAction` contracts are deployed together and not separately, as is done when using DarkSpells. Validators must perform the following two checks:

1. Check that the DssAction contract’s `execute()` function only calls the `actions()` function and does not interact with any external contracts or explicitly defined Ethereum addresses.
2. Check that the second argument used in the constructor when instantiating the `DssExec` is a newly created Spell action contract (e.g. `address(new DssSpellAction())`) and not an explicitly defined Ethereum address. This confirms that the Spell is linked to the correct action contract.

If either of these checks fails, the Spell cannot pass validation.

The validation checks can be performed by navigating to the "Contract tab" on Etherscan for the deployed Spell. In the source code, first locate the `DssAction` contract (or its equivalent, such as `DssSpellAction`). Review the `execute()` function and make sure that it only calls the `actions()` function. Then, locate the constructor and confirm that the `action` argument is instantiated as a new contract.

assessments.title: Spell Validators Must Perform Basic Spell Code Validation
assessments.quote:

Validators should look for any unusual behavior, such as:

- Low-level assembly operations (e.g., `assembly` blocks).
- The use of Solidity opcodes, such as `delegatecall`, `callcode`, or `selfdestruct`.
- Suspicious-looking payments or transfers.
- Any other malicious or unauthorized code. This includes cross-checking the Solidity code in `actions()` against the Executive Sheet and the Executive Document. Each action must be authorized per the Atlas.

Spell validators must report any code they find that appears to be malicious or which likely forms part of an attempted attack. A Spell must not pass validation if the Spell validator is convinced that malicious code is present in a Spell or that its execution can lead to an attack on the Sky Protocol.

To perform this validation, the validator must go to the "Contract" tab on Etherscan and review the source code.

assessments.title: Spell Validators Should Validate Executive Document
assessments.quote:
The Spell validator should confirm that the smart contract developers referenced the correct governance copy when building the Spell and that the document voters see on the Voting Portal matches the Spell contents. This is done by verifying that the hash in the Spell corresponds to the version of the Executive Document stored in the GitHub repository.

To perform this validation, the validator must first locate the Executive Hash, which can be found on the voting platform under "Spell Details" for the Executive Vote. Validators should be aware that the hash refers to an earlier commit of the Executive Document markdown, prior to the inclusion of the contract address. After validating the hash against this earlier commit, validators must conduct a diff check between the commit associated with the Executive Hash and the final version of the document to confirm that the only difference is the replacement of the Spell address placeholder.

The check can be performed in two ways:

1. Using an Online Tool:
    - Copy and paste the body of the Executive Document from GitHub into the online Keccak-256 hash generator tool ([https://emn178.github.io/online-tools/keccak_256.html](https://emn178.github.io/online-tools/keccak_256.html)).
    - Compare the generated hash with the hash included in the Spell.
2. Using `cast`
    - Generate the hash directly from the raw GitHub URL at the specific commit:
        - Run the following command to generate the hash: `cast keccak -- "$(wget $RAW_EXEC_URL -O -)"`
        - Use the raw file URL at the specific commit.
    - Compare the generated hash with the hash included in the Spell.
assessments.description: Requires Spell validators to verify the Spell's Executive Document hash against the GitHub commit and confirm the voter-facing document matches.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The core check is objective: the Keccak-256 hash in the Spell must equal the hash of the referenced commit, and the diff must show only the Spell address placeholder replacement. assessments.title: Spell Validators Should Review Constants
assessments.quote:
Validators should ensure that the rates are defined as per-second accumulation values, using the correct precision units common in the Sky Protocol (e.g., RAY for rates, RAD for debt/DAI amounts, WAD for general token amounts).

**Precision Units Overview**:

- **WAD (10^18)**: Used for token amounts and balances.
- **RAD (10^45)**: Used for debt values, ceilings, or large accumulations.
- **RAY (10^27)**: Used for rates and multipliers.

These units prevent floating-point issues in Solidity — always confirm they're applied correctly to avoid overflows or miscalculations. Group this with general constant validations (e.g., ensuring hardcoded values like fees or ceilings are computed accurately).

Rate values can be validated against the commented rate by using the `bc` command in a bash shell. Using the `NEW_FEE` variable in the example contract the following is visible: `bc -l <<< 'scale=27; e( l(1.095)/(60 * 60 * 24 * 365) )`. This produces 1.000000002877801985002875644. Removing the decimal place will allow you to see that this matches the definition of `NEW_FEE`.

Validating all rate adjustments can be done the same way. For more information on the rates module, refer to the developer guide ([https://github.com/sky-ecosystem/developerguides/blob/master/mcd/intro-rate-mechanism/intro-rate-mechanism.md](https://github.com/sky-ecosystem/developerguides/blob/master/mcd/intro-rate-mechanism/intro-rate-mechanism.md)). For easy reference, common pre-computed rates can also be viewed at the following ipfs link ([https://ipfs.io/ipfs/QmefQMseb3AiTapiAKKexdKHig8wroKuZbmLtPLv4u2YwW](https://ipfs.io/ipfs/QmefQMseb3AiTapiAKKexdKHig8wroKuZbmLtPLv4u2YwW)).

Immediately prior to making rate changes, `drip` must be called on the respective contracts.

The drip requirement is immediate but has no defined timing window.

assessments.title: Spell Validators Should Review Contract For Unusual Elements
assessments.quote:
Validators should assess whether any unusual or unexpected elements appear in the contract. It could be:

- Hidden state changes: Look for retrieval functions (e.g., `get` or `view`) that include assignments (`=`), indicating state changes.
- External Calls At The End: Check for external calls (e.g., `.call`, `.send`, `.transfer`) made after state changes, as this could indicate potential reentrancy attacks.
- Force Ether, DAI or SKY Reception: Look for a `receive` function with no logic, which could forcibly receive assets.
- Use of `tx.origin`: The tx.origin variable refers to the address that started the current transaction. If `tx.origin` is used instead of `msg.sender` in decision-making processes, it could lead to unintended authorization.
- Function Naming Overlaps: A contract might have function names that are similar or overlap with common Solidity functions to mislead a reviewer. Check for misleading function names (e.g., `transfer`, `approve`, `mint`) with unexpected logic or assignments.

To perform this validation the validator must go to the "Contract" tab on Etherscan and review the source code.
assessments.description: Directs Ecosystem Validators to review spell contract source on Etherscan for listed unusual patterns such as tx.origin misuse and misleading function names.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The obligation to 'assess whether any unusual or unexpected elements appear' is judgment language, and the listed checks are introduced with 'It could be', so they read as illustrative rather than pass/fail criteria. No thresholds, cadence, or deadline are stated, though the named review location (Etherscan Contract tab) and the concrete code patterns give some verifiability.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: No mechanism reaches the validator's review duty. Emergency Spells (b8266c11) could respond to a malicious spell that slips through, but that remedies the threat rather than penalizing a validator who skipped or botched the review, and no penalty or escalation for validators is stated.

Validators should check the following:

- Ensure that all dependencies in the Spell repository (e.g., imported libraries like dss-exec-lib or git submodules) are current and up to date with the Spell. To perform this check the validator must browse or clone the GitHub repository (e.g., Spells-mainnet). Review Solidity files (e.g., in src/) for import statements, check the .gitmodules file for submodules, and run `git submodule status` to verify versions. Compare against source repositories for updates, then test with `make test` to confirm compatibility. The source repository can be identified in the Spell's source code, as the imported library or dependency is followed by "from", which points to the source path (e.g., `import {GemAbstract} from "dss-interfaces/ERC/GemAbstract.sol";` points to dss-interfaces.)
- Verify that the test scripts themselves have not been tampered with or maliciously modified in the repository.
- Confirm that the Spell repository branch matches the branch specified in the pull request or governance proposal.

assessments.title: Spell Validators Should Verify The Contract ABI
assessments.quote:
Validators should verify that the contract ABI (Application Binary Interface) is correctly generated and matches the deployed contract.

To perform this check, the validator must go to the "Contract" tab on Etherscan and the "Contract ABI" section. Copy the ABI JSON and compare it against the expected ABI from the official GitHub repository (e.g., Spells-mainnet repo). To obtain the expected ABI from the GitHub repository download the relevant Solidity file, paste it into a tool like Remix IDE, select the matching compiler version, and compile to extract the ABI JSON. Use a diff tool to check for exact matches in functions, parameters, and types.
assessments.description: Directs Spell Validators to verify on Etherscan and via a Remix compile that a spell's contract ABI matches the expected ABI from the GitHub repository.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The procedure names concrete steps, tools, and a matching criterion (exact match of functions, parameters, and types). However, the core obligation uses 'should', and no deadline, cadence, or consequence is defined for a mismatch or for skipping the check.

Compiler version must match the deployed contract's compiler version
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. Penalty Mechanisms and Risk-Based Insurance Pricing target Primes and Operational Agents, not Ecosystem Validators. Emergency Spells could respond to a threatened security rule but do not reach a validator's failure to perform the check. Only the misalignment catch-all applies.

assessments.title: Spell Validators Should Check For Hidden Or Unverified Contracts
assessments.quote:
Validators should check for hidden or unverified contracts linked to the Spell (e.g., libraries or proxies).

To perform these checks, the validator must go to the "Contract" tab on Etherscan and review the source code. Scan the code for any referenced contracts or addresses: Look for imports, inherited contracts, hardcoded addresses, or function calls to external contracts. If it's an address, search it directly on Etherscan and confirm it's verified (e.g., green checkmark with available source code). Compare the referenced code to the official GitHub repository (e.g., Spells-mainnet repo) to ensure versions match and nothing has been altered.
assessments.description: Requires Ecosystem Validators to check Spell-linked contracts on Etherscan for verification and compare their code against the official GitHub repository.

However, it uses advisory 'should' language, 'e.g.' examples, and no cadence or pass/fail threshold for 'nothing has been altered'.
metrics: Each referenced contract or address must be verified on Etherscan (green checkmark with available source code)
Referenced code must match the official GitHub repository versions with nothing altered
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. Emergency Spells (b8266c11) address spells that threaten security rather than a validator omitting these checks, and no penalty or escalation is tied to validator performance. Only the misalignment and adjudication catch-alls apply.

assessments.title: Validation Outcome Reporting
assessments.quote: The Spell validator is responsible for reporting the outcome of the validation process. This includes determining whether the Spell passes or fails validation, documenting any issues discovered during the validation process, and ensuring that all issues are resolved before the Spell can be classified as passing validation. The process for reporting, including how to report and to whom issues should be reported, is detailed in the subdocuments herein.
assessments.description: Requires the Spell validator to report pass/fail outcomes, document discovered issues, and resolve all issues before a Spell passes.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The paragraph names a responsible actor and enumerates three obligations, including a pass gate. However, it gives no criteria for what counts as an issue, what counts as resolved, or any deadline or documentation format, and it defers the reporting details to subdocuments.

assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. The paragraph does not link the validator's reporting duty to any on-chain gate, penalty, or escalation path. Penalty Mechanisms (b8ee2d12) target Primes and Operational Agents rather than Ecosystem Validators, and Emergency Spells (b8266c11) are not tied to this reporting duty, so only the catch-all backstop would apply.

assessments.title: Spell Passing Validation
assessments.quote:
A Spell is classified as passing validation when:

1. All validation checks are completed without identifying issues, or
2. All reported issues have been resolved to the satisfaction of the Spell validator

Validation of the Spell should ideally be public, though this is not mandatory.
assessments.description: Defines when a Spell counts as passing validation, via no-issues or issues-resolved-to-validator-satisfaction criteria.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The two passing conditions are judgment-based: 'all validation checks' is never enumerated, and 'resolved to the satisfaction of the Spell validator' delegates the outcome to one party's discretion. No thresholds, cadence, or deadlines appear, and the public-validation language is expressly non-mandatory.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. The paragraph does not tie passing validation to any consequence, and no citable mechanism (penalty, conservatorship, emergency spell, or on-chain gate) is shown to reach it. Only the catch-all misalignment and adjudication backstops could apply.

assessments.title: Spell Failing Validation
assessments.quote:
A Spell is classified as failing validation when:

1. One or more issues are identified during validation, or
2. Reported issues remain unresolved to the satisfaction of the Spell validator.
assessments.description: Defines when a Spell is classified as failing validation: identified issues or unresolved reported issues.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The first condition ('one or more issues') sets a count threshold, but 'issues' is never defined. The second condition turns on whether reported issues are resolved 'to the satisfaction of the Spell validator', a subjective standard with no objective criteria, so compliance is arguable either way.

Reported issues unresolved to the satisfaction of the Spell validator constitutes failing validation
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. The paragraph only classifies a Spell's status, and no catalog mechanism checks or penalizes the validator's classification judgment. The only backstop is the generic misalignment and adjudication machinery, which is a catch-all.

assessments.title: Reporting Issues Found During Validation
assessments.quote:
Issues discovered during validation must be reported as follows:

1. Mandatory Reporting: If the validation check is required, the issue must be reported immediately.
2. Recommended Reporting: If the validation check is recommended, validators are strongly encouraged to report issues unless they are certain the issue is not malicious, a bug, or an attack on the Sky Protocol.
3. Out-of-Scope Issues: Any issues found outside the scope of validation checks should also be reported as soon as it is found.

In general, any issue that appears functional or potentially functional should be reported.
assessments.description: Requires validators to report issues found during spell validation, with immediate reporting for mandatory checks and encouraged reporting otherwise.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: "Immediately" and "as soon as it is found" give a timing standard, but no reporting channel, recipient, or deadline is defined. "Strongly encouraged", "certain the issue is not malicious", and "appears functional or potentially functional" are judgment standards, so a validator could plausibly argue either compliance or non-compliance on the same facts.
metrics: Mandatory validation check issues must be reported immediately
Out-of-scope issues must be reported as soon as found
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No penalty, conservatorship, or emergency mechanism is tied to validators failing to report issues, and the only generic backstop is the misalignment reporting catch-all, which is weak on its own.

assessments.title: Resolving Issues
assessments.quote:
When an issue has been reported by a Spell validator, the Core Facilitator or the Spell Team who worked on the Spell is likely to respond to the issue. The Spell validator must assume that the parties providing the answer are acting maliciously and lying to prevent the discovery of their attack.

The validator may only consider the issue as resolved once they are comfortable that the issue does not constitute a bug or attack that poses a threat to the Sky Protocol. Only the validator who raised the issue is permitted to consider an issue as resolved, and any unresolved issue will prevent the Spell from passing validation.
assessments.description: Governs how a Spell validator resolves reported issues, and states that any unresolved issue blocks the Spell from passing validation.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The blocking rule is concrete: an unresolved issue prevents Spell validation from passing, and only the raising validator may resolve it. The resolution standard is judgmental, though: the validator must be "comfortable" the issue is not a threat, with no defined test, evidence threshold, or cadence, so compliance is arguable.
metrics: Any unresolved issue prevents the Spell from passing validation (binary gate)
Only the validator who raised the issue may mark it resolved
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. The validation block is a process gate with no penalty, escalation, or on-chain enforcement attached, and the raising validator self-certifies resolution, which is self-enforcement. The catch-all misalignment and adjudication mechanisms alone do not reach this rule.

Private reporting of issues can be performed using platforms such as Slack or Signal.

assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. The paragraph is a non-binding recommendation with no penalty, escalation, or enforcer attached; no catalog mechanism reaches a choice of reporting channel, so only self-enforcement by the validator applies.

assessments.title: Public Validation Status Reporting
assessments.quote: Publicly reporting issues found during Spell validation is the recommended method of issue reporting. Issues reported publicly may be reported to the Core Facilitator on the Sky Forum.
assessments.description: Recommends publicly reporting Spell validation issues, optionally to the Core Facilitator on the Sky Forum.

assessments.title: Outcome Of The Executive Proposal Vote
assessments.quote: When an Executive Proposal is ready for a vote by Sky Governance, SKY holders cast their votes. The voting process determines whether the Executive Proposal gains enough support to move forward to the execution phase. If the executive does not accumulate sufficient SKY to "move the hat" (i.e., reach the required threshold for approval), it does not proceed to execution immediately; however, it can still gain support and be executed later within the expiration window. For official Spells, there is a 30-day expiration period after deployment. Once this period lapses, the Spell process ends, and no further actions can be taken for the associated Spell. If the executive gains enough support to be approved, the process moves forward to the execution phase.
assessments.description: Describes SKY-holder voting on Executive Proposals, with a 30-day expiration window for official Spells before execution lapses.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The 30-day expiration period after deployment for official Spells is a concrete, verifiable deadline. The approval threshold is only described as reaching 'enough' SKY, with no quantity or formula stated, so the core gating criterion is delegated.
metrics: Official Spells expire 30 days after deployment
assessments.enforcementReasoning: No consequence for a failed or late vote is stated, and no catalog mechanism reaches this rule. The expiration is a timing constraint rather than a penalty, so none found.

assessments.title: Lifting the Spell
assessments.quote: Before a Spell can be scheduled for execution, it must be "lifted" to become the active "hat" in the DSChief contract. To lift a Spell, that Spell must have more approvals than the current hat. This action is permissionless, meaning any Ethereum address can trigger the execution without requiring special permissions.
assessments.description: Requires a Spell to have more approvals than the current hat before it can be lifted in DSChief, which anyone may trigger.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The operative condition is a concrete, checkable comparison (more approvals than the current hat) and the actor scope is explicit (any Ethereum address). The paragraph does not state the unit of approvals or the measurement point, and it leaves the hat-replacement mechanics to the DSChief contract rather than the text.

Lifting is permissionless: any Ethereum address may trigger it
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. The DSChief contract's approval comparison is on-chain and self-executing, but no catalog mechanism or UUID in the paragraph covers this lift precondition, so it cannot be cited as an enforcement path.

assessments.title: Chief-keeper
assessments.quote: The chief-keeper monitors and interacts with DSChief and DSSSpells. When a Spell receives more approval than the current hat, the chief-keeper calls the `lift` function to make this Spell the new hat. After confirming hat status, the chief-keeper proceeds to schedule the Spell, ensuring that only the current hat is scheduled for execution.
assessments.description: Requires the chief-keeper to lift a spell that out-polls the current hat and schedule only the hat for execution.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The trigger is concrete: a spell with more approval than the current hat must be lifted via the `lift` function, and only the hat may be scheduled. However, "monitors" has no cadence, and there is no deadline for lifting or scheduling.
metrics: Spell approval greater than current hat approval triggers a call to `lift`
Only the current hat is scheduled for execution
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No penalty, conservatorship, or emergency mechanism is tied to chief-keeper hat handling. The DSChief contract logic is not a cited catalog mechanism, and the paragraph does not reference any enforcer besides the actor itself.

assessments.title: Execution Setup For Approved Vote
assessments.quote:
If the executive is approved and has been lifted to become the current hat in the DSChief, a future action to execute the Spell's actions is prepared by calling `schedule()` on the Spell contract. This action is permissionless, meaning any Ethereum address can trigger the execution without requiring special permissions. This process involves calling `plot` on `ds-pause` with four parameters related to the Spell action contract:

- The address of the Spell action contract.
- The `extcodehash` value of the Spell action contract.
- Any `calldata` information required for the future execution of the Spell contract's actions using `execute()`.
- The `eta`, which is the earliest time the Spell's actions can be executed. This must be scheduled at least the duration of the pause delay into the future.

Once the Spell's actions are "plotted" in the Pause, the Spell is considered `scheduled`, and the countdown to the `eta` time begins. In the absence of Office Hours, this countdown is typically equal to the duration of the `GSM Pause Delay`. If Office Hours are set to "Yes" then the countdown will be equal to the `GSM Pause Delay` plus whatever time is needed to enter the Office Hours window.
assessments.description: Specifies how an approved executive spell is scheduled via permissionless schedule() and plot() on ds-pause, with eta and countdown rules.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The eta must be at least the pause delay into the future, and the countdown equals the GSM Pause Delay absent Office Hours, which gives a checkable formula. The GSM Pause Delay value is defined elsewhere, and the Office Hours extension is left open-ended ("whatever time is needed").
metrics: eta scheduled at least the duration of the pause delay into the future
countdown to eta typically equal to GSM Pause Delay when Office Hours are not in effect
with Office Hours set to Yes, countdown equals GSM Pause Delay plus time needed to enter the Office Hours window
assessments.enforcementReasoning: The pause delay is a timelock, but no catalog mechanism for it is cited, and the paragraph carries no UUID. Emergency Spells can pre-authorize halting a plotted spell during the delay window if an improper scheduling is detected, which plausibly reaches a violation, but the consequence is not quantified for this rule.

assessments.title: Casting And Execution Of Approved Spell
assessments.quote: Once the current time exceeds the `eta` value set during scheduling, the Spell can be `cast` (see [A.1.10.2.4.13.3 - Execution Setup For Approved Vote](e06f6a83-7c74-4abd-b4da-771cbfdf2fb9)). Casting and the subsequent execution path occur atomically within the same transaction. This entire process is permissionless, meaning any Ethereum address can trigger the execution without requiring special permissions.
assessments.description: Specifies that an approved spell may be cast once its eta has passed, with casting and execution atomic and permissionless.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The core condition is objective and checkable: casting is allowed only once current time exceeds the scheduled eta, and casting and execution occur in one transaction. Gaps remain: the eta value's source and expiry or grace period are not stated here.
metrics: Casting allowed only once current time exceeds the eta value set during scheduling
Casting and subsequent execution occur atomically within the same transaction
Any Ethereum address may trigger execution (permissionless)
assessments.enforcementReasoning: The eta gate is a timelock enforced by contract code, so premature casting is structurally blocked, but the paragraph does not state that as a consequence. Emergency Spells (b8266c11) can halt a scheduled spell before cast, which plausibly reaches a threat to this path, but the escalation is not quantified for this rule.

assessments.title: Casting Of Spell
assessments.quote:
When the `cast` function in the DssSpell contract is called:

- The Spell is marked as `cast`, preventing it from being executed again.
- The `cast` function initiates the execution process by calling the `exec` function in the `ds-pause` contract.
assessments.description: Specifies that calling cast on a DssSpell marks the spell as cast to prevent re-execution and triggers exec in ds-pause.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The paragraph names concrete contract functions (cast, exec, ds-pause) and enumerates two deterministic steps that code review could verify. It states no numeric thresholds, deadlines, or parameter values, so the behavior is precise but not quantified.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. The one-time-cast guard is enforced by contract code, but no catalog mechanism or UUID in the text is cited that reaches this rule; Emergency Spells (b8266c11) concerns emergency interventions, not the cast/exec sequence.

assessments.title: Execution Of Spell
assessments.quote:
Within the same transaction initiated by `cast()`, ds-pause proceeds as follows:

1. Validation and Removal: The `exec` function in `ds-pause` validates the execution request and removes it from the list of scheduled executions.
2. Delegate Call to Spell Action Contract: The `ds-pause` contract calls `exec` on the Pause Proxy contract, which performs a `delegatecall` to the Spell action contract address specified during scheduling.
3. Execution of Spell Actions:
    - For regular Spells, the Pause Proxy calls the `execute()` function on the `DssSpellAction` contract.
    - The `execute()` function calls the `actions()` function, where the Spell’s actions are carried out.
4. Error Handling: If the transaction reverts at any point (e.g., due to an error in `actions()`), the Pause Proxy halts execution.
5. Final Checks: If the transaction succeeds, the `exec` function in `ds-pause` performs a final ownership check to ensure the Pause Proxy is still owned by `ds-pause`.
6. Completion: Once the final check passes, the execution of `cast()` is finalized, marking the end of the process.
assessments.description: Specifies the ds-pause execution sequence for a scheduled spell, from validation through delegatecall, actions, revert handling, and ownership check.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: Names the functions (exec, cast, execute, actions), the delegatecall target, and an ordered six-step sequence that a third party could check against the code. It lacks timing or cadence and leaves some revert and failure scope loosely described ("at any point").
assessments.enforcementReasoning: Atomic transaction reversion halts a failing run, but it does not reach skipped or altered steps. No catalog mechanism (Emergency Spells, Penalty Mechanisms, and so on) is shown to police this sequence, so none found.

The updates must be completed in a timely manner following Spell execution, and must not introduce changes beyond those necessitated by the Spell outcome.

assessments.title: Continuous Approval Voting
assessments.quote:
Executive Votes operate under a Continuous Approval Voting mechanism. Voters can support multiple proposals by allocating their SKY vote-weight to each, with the goal of helping a favored proposal surpass the current "hat"—the proposal with the most approval in the DSChief contract. Voters can apply their full SKY vote-weight to up to 5 different proposals simultaneously (as defined by the `max_yays` limit in the contract), rather than splitting their tokens between them. If SKY token holders disagree with a new proposal, they can redirect their SKY vote-weight to the inactive proposal with the highest vote-weight (often the last successfully passed proposal) to maintain the status quo or support an alternative. An active proposal can become the hat if it accumulates more votes than any other, including the current hat, at which point it is "lifted" to become the new hat. This lifting process marks the active proposal, and it may now be scheduled and later executed, provided it meets other conditions like the GSM Pause Delay. There are three key aspects to Continuous Approval Voting:
- Victory threshold set by the hat: The vote-weight on the current hat proposal establishes the "victory threshold" that new proposals must exceed to become eligible for execution. This ensures only the most supported changes advance.
- Dynamic vote-weight movement: Vote-weight can shift from the hat to a new proposal, simultaneously lowering the victory threshold for the hat while boosting the new proposal's chances. This fluidity allows for real-time community consensus shifts.
- Securing the hat: Vote-weight is encouraged to remain on the hat proposal even after it's lifted, acting as a security measure against "rogue" or less-supported proposals that might attempt to overtake it with minimal backing.
assessments.description: Describes Continuous Approval Voting for Executive Votes, including the five-proposal cap, the hat victory threshold, and vote-weight movement.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The five-proposal cap (max_yays) and the hat-based victory threshold (most votes wins the hat) are concrete and checkable against DSChief. The GSM Pause Delay is referenced without a value, and the 'securing the hat' aspect is only 'encouraged', so it is non-binding.
